w: Antwerp's memory bank, going back to 1481. Renamed for Flemish novelist Hendrik Conscience, whose statue stands guard outside, the library holds over a million volumes — early printed books from before 1830, Flemish folklore, and everything ever written about the city itself, Antverpiensia and all.
_facts: Repository library of the city of Antwerp, with history going back to 1481
Named after Flemish writer Hendrik Conscience, whose statue adorns the library
Collection of over one million books, including pre-1830 early printed works and Flemish folk culture

w: One street, half of Asia. Chinese settlers who arrived after World War II built this into Antwerp's Chinatown — stone lions guarding both ends, a Buddhist temple, a kung fu school, and Sun Wah, the country's biggest Asian supermarket. A pagoda gate went up in 2010 after four years of planning.
s: Antwerp's Chinatown, one street, pagoda gate and all
_facts: Street historically supporting the Chinese community that settled in Antwerp after World War II
Home to Sun Wah, the biggest Asian supermarket in the country, plus a Buddhist temple and a kung fu school
Chinese lions guard the entrance and end of the street
A Pagoda Gate (Pagodepoort) was erected in 2010 after four years of planning

w: Two Antwerp grandees' houses, knocked into one museum. Painter Frans Snyders and city mayor Nicolaas Rockox once lived next door to each other; their combined townhouses now hold a collection of 16th- and 17th-century Flemish art, kept alive today under the stewardship of KBC Bank.
s: A painter and a mayor's houses, joined as one museum
_facts: Museum in two neighbouring townhouses formerly owned by painter Frans Snyders and mayor Nicolaas Rockox
Owned by KBC Bank
Showcases a collection of 16th and 17th century Flemish art

n: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp
w: A neoclassical palace of paintings built on the bones of a demolished citadel. Founded in 1810 and completed in 1894, the museum's facade carries bronze chariots and medallions of the city's own masters — van Eyck, Rubens and Quentin Matsys among them — a five-century collection housed in a monument to itself.
s: Neoclassical palace of art on a demolished citadel
_facts: Founded in 1810, houses paintings, sculptures and drawings from the 14th to 20th centuries
Neoclassical building, landmark of the Zuid district, opened 1890 and completed 1894
Built on the former site of the Antwerp Citadel
Facade includes bronze sculptures and medallions of artists including Jan van Eyck and Rubens

w: Rubens designed his own house the way he painted — big, Italianate, unmistakably his. He bought the Antwerp townhouse in 1610 and rebuilt it to his own designs, giving it the courtyard swagger of an Italian palazzo. Now a museum of his work and circle, the artist's residence itself is currently closed for restoration.
s: Rubens designed his own Italianate townhouse
_facts: Former home and workshop of Peter Paul Rubens, purchased in 1610
Renovated and extended to designs by Rubens himself, giving it an Italian-palazzo look
Now a museum dedicated to Rubens and his contemporaries
Main Artist's Residence section closed for renovation as of November 2025

w: One of the oldest zoos on Earth, and it never left downtown. Established on 21 July 1843, Antwerp Zoo has spent close to two centuries wedged right next to Antwerpen-Centraal railway station — animals and arrivals sharing the same corner of the city ever since.
s: One of the world's oldest zoos, still downtown
_facts: Oldest animal park in Belgium and one of the oldest in the world
Established on 21 July 1843
Located next to Antwerpen-Centraal railway station in the city centre

w: The 'Farmers' Tower' that out-built almost everything but a cathedral. Raised between 1929 and 1932, this Art Deco high-rise was Europe's second-tallest building by roof height at completion, beaten only by Madrid's Telefonica Building. It stayed Antwerp's tallest structure bar the Gothic cathedral spire until 2019.
_facts: Historic Art Deco high-rise, officially the KBC Tower, constructed 1929-1932
One of Europe's very first tall buildings, designed by Jan Vanhoenacker, Emile Van Averbeke and Jos Smolderen
Second tallest building in Europe by roof height at construction, after Madrid's Telefonica Building
Remained Antwerp's tallest structure (after the cathedral) until surpassed by Antwerp Tower in 2019

w: Built for pilgrims heading to Santiago de Compostela, and still on their route today. Behind its Brabantine Gothic walls, St. James' packs in two dozen Baroque altars and paintings by Rubens, Jordaens and Maerten de Vos. Rubens himself is buried here, alongside his wife Helena Fourment.
s: Pilgrim church where Rubens himself is buried
_facts: Former collegiate church built on the site of a hostel and chapel for pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela
Brabantine Gothic design with a rich Baroque interior, 24 altars
Holds paintings by Rubens, Jacob Jordaens and Maerten de Vos
Burial place of Peter Paul Rubens and his wife Helena Fourment

w: Antwerp's Jewish community traces back to the 14th century, but this synagogue is younger and grander. Built in 1893 by descendants of Dutch Jewish settlers, the Hollandse Synagoge on Bouwmeestersstraat was the city's first large synagogue — still an Orthodox congregation more than a century on.
_facts: Orthodox Jewish congregation and synagogue on Bouwmeestersstraat, officially Synagogue Shomre Hadas
First Jews arrived in Antwerp in the 14th century, though the congregation was formally established in 1816
Built in 1893 by descendants of Jews who came from the Netherlands in the early 19th century
The first large synagogue in Antwerp
